claim: Co-culture of human cells expressing the receptor ACE2 with cells expressing SARS-CoV-2 spike results in synapse-like intercellular contacts that initiate cell-cell fusion.
source: Here, we report that co-culture of human cells expressing the receptor ACE2 with cells expressing SARS-CoV-2 spike, results in synapse-like intercellular contacts that initiate cell-cell fusion, producing syncytia resembling those we identify in lungs of COVID-19 patients.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and related text describing live cell microscopy observations of spike-ACE2 interactions leading to fusion.

claim: Syncytia produced by spike-ACE2 co-culture resemble those identified in lungs of COVID-19 patients.
source: Here, we report that co-culture of human cells expressing the receptor ACE2 with cells expressing SARS-CoV-2 spike, results in synapse-like intercellular contacts that initiate cell-cell fusion, producing syncytia resembling those we identify in lungs of COVID-19 patients.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by histological examination of lung tissue from COVID-19 patients showing multinucleated syncytia (Figure 2D-H).

claim: A high-throughput screen of ~6000 drugs reveals an essential role for cholesterol-rich regions in spike-mediated fusion.
source: To assess the mechanism of spike/ACE2-driven membrane fusion, we developed a microscopy-based, cell-cell fusion assay to screen ~6000 drugs and >30 spike variants. Together with quantitative cell biology approaches, the screen reveals an essential role for biophysical aspects of the membrane, particularly cholesterol-rich regions, in spike-mediated fusion, which extends to replication-competent SARS-CoV-2 isolates.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data from the drug screen (Figure 4) and cholesterol depletion experiments (Figures 6-7).

claim: The essential role of cholesterol-rich regions in spike-mediated fusion extends to replication-competent SARS-CoV-2 isolates.
source: Together with quantitative cell biology approaches, the screen reveals an essential role for biophysical aspects of the membrane, particularly cholesterol-rich regions, in spike-mediated fusion, which extends to replication-competent SARS-CoV-2 isolates.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by experiments with SARS-CoV-2 clinical isolates showing that viral cholesterol depletion blocks infection (Figure 7F-G).

claim: COVID-19 has caused over a million deaths in the year following identification of SARS-CoV-2.
source: COVID-19 has caused over a million deaths in the year following identification of its causative pathogen, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) (Zhu et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is a factual statement cited from literature (Zhu et al., 2020a).

claim: Trimeric spike glycoproteins give the viral envelope its crown-like appearance.
source: Central to these efforts are trimeric spike glycoproteins (or 'peplomers'), which give the viral envelope its crown-like appearance, and ACE2, their essential human receptor (Duan et al., 2020; Mittal et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to established literature (Duan et al., 2020; Mittal et al., 2020).

claim: ACE2 is the essential human receptor for SARS-CoV-2 spike protein.
source: Central to these efforts are trimeric spike glycoproteins (or 'peplomers'), which give the viral envelope its crown-like appearance, and ACE2, their essential human receptor (Duan et al., 2020; Mittal et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to established literature (Duan et al., 2020; Mittal et al., 2020).

claim: Association of spike and ACE2 proteins underlies virus-cell adhesion, which precedes a conformational change in spike that unleashes its fusion machinery.
source: Association of the two proteins underlies virus-cell adhesion, which precedes a conformational change in spike that unleashes its fusion machinery to infiltrate the cell (Hoffmann et al., 2020a; Hoffmann et al., 2020b; Ke et al., 2020; Lan et al., 2020; Shang et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Viral proteins may feature an intrinsic preference for membrane domains of distinct lipid composition.
source: While cargo receptor-binding likely plays a role, an alternative possibility is that such proteins feature an intrinsic preference for membrane domains of distinct lipid composition (Cattin-Ortolá et al., 2020; Li et al., 2007; Liao et al., 2006; Lu et al., 2008a; McBride et al., 2007; Thorp and Gallagher, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the introduction and supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Certain viruses require association between receptor proteins and specific lipids to trigger endocytosis.
source: Indeed, certain viruses require association between receptor proteins and specific lipids to trigger endocytosis (Levental et al., 2020; Pelkmans, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to established literature (Levental et al., 2020; Pelkmans, 2005).

claim: Infection by many enveloped viruses causes fusogenic viral protein display on the host cell plasma membrane, allowing neighboring cells to fuse into multinucleated syncytia.
source: For many enveloped viruses, infection indeed causes fusogenic viral protein display on the host cell plasma membrane, which allows neighboring cells to fuse into multinucleated 'syncytia' (Ciechonska and Duncan, 2014; Compton and Schwartz, 2017; Duelli and Lazebnik, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Cell-cell fusion can play key roles in viral pathogenicity, including viral replication and evasion of the host immune response.
source: Past studies of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and others suggest that cell-cell fusion can play key roles in pathogenicity, whether it be in viral replication, or evasion of the host immune response (Frankel et al., 1996; Johnson et al., 2007; Maudgal and Missotten, 1978).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to established literature on RSV and HIV.

claim: Recent studies on SARS-CoV-2 identified syncytia similar to those observed in SARS-CoV-1.
source: Pioneering work on SARS-CoV-1 (Li et al., 2003) as well as recent studies on SARS-CoV-2 identified similar syncytia (Buchrieser et al., 2020; Cattin-Ortolá et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2020a; Ou et al., 2020; Papa et al., 2020; Xia et al., 2020; Zang et al., 2020b), which may or may not be relevant to patient pathology (Bryce et al., 2020; Giacca et al., 2020; Rockx et al., 2020; Tian et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: ACE2-spike clusters assemble at transcellular, synapse-like contacts, which precede fusion pore formation and multinucleation.
source: Mechanistically, ACE2-spike clusters assemble at transcellular, synapse-like contacts, which precede fusion pore formation and multinucleation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by live cell microscopy data shown in Figure 1D-I.

claim: Contact between spike-expressing and ACE2-expressing cells results in near instantaneous accumulation of spike protein clusters at ACE2-containing membrane protrusions.
source: Invariably, contact between opposite cell types (spike vs. ACE2) results in near instantaneous accumulation of spike protein clusters at ACE2-containing membrane protrusions (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by live cell microscopy data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Spike-ACE2 punctate structures are long-lived (minutes), similar to physiological synapses.
source: These punctate structures are long-lived (minutes) (Figure 1-video 1), similar to physiological synapses (e.g. neuronal, immunological) (Cohen and Ziv, 2019; Dustin, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by live cell microscopy data (Figure 1-video 1) and comparison to literature on physiological synapses.

claim: Fusion events proceed from spike-ACE2 synapses, often within a few minutes of their formation.
source: In all observed cases, fusion events proceed from such synapses (Figure 1E–F; Figure 1—video 2), often within a few minutes of their formation, but frequently following longer durations of time.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by live cell microscopy data shown in Figure 1E-F and Figure 1-video 2.

claim: In most cases, fusion pore dilation follows retraction of an individual spike cluster toward the interior of an ACE2 cell.
source: In most (but not all) examples, fusion pore dilation follows retraction of an individual spike cluster toward the interior of an ACE2 cell (Figure 1F–I), suggesting that motility-associated mechanical forces (e.g. actomyosin contractility) and/or endocytosis is pivotal to overcoming the energetic barrier to lipid bilayer mixing.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by live cell microscopy data shown in Figure 1F-I.

claim: Motility-associated mechanical forces and/or endocytosis may be pivotal to overcoming the energetic barrier to lipid bilayer mixing during fusion.
source: In most (but not all) examples, fusion pore dilation follows retraction of an individual spike cluster toward the interior of an ACE2 cell (Figure 1F–I), suggesting that motility-associated mechanical forces (e.g. actomyosin contractility) and/or endocytosis is pivotal to overcoming the energetic barrier to lipid bilayer mixing.
evidence: This is stated as an inference in the Results section based on observations of spike cluster retraction preceding fusion.

claim: Most primary fusion events occur within 60 minutes when cells are plated at high density.
source: When cells are plated at high density, most 'primary' fusion events occur within 60 min (Figure 1G–J), with latter 'secondary' amalgamation of small syncytia into progressively larger structures (Figure 1K; Figure 1—video 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by live cell microscopy data shown in Figure 1G-J.

claim: Over time, syncytia undergo vacuolization, likely from fusion-driven collapse of intracellular organelles into hybrid compartments.
source: Over time, syncytia undergo vacuolization, likely from fusion-driven collapse of intracellular organelles into hybrid compartments (Figure 1L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: By 48-72 hours, syncytia disintegrate into immobile spike/ACE2-coated vesicles.
source: By 48–72 hr, cells disintegrate into immobile spike/ACE2-coated vesicles, having eaten themselves from within (Figure 1M).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1M.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 spike is a particularly potent mediator of syncytia formation relative to SARS-CoV-1 spike and commonly studied fusogens.
source: Intriguingly, SARS-CoV-2 spike is a particularly potent mediator of syncytia formation relative to both SARS-CoV-1 spike and commonly studied fusogens (e.g. p14 FAST, MYMK/MYMX) (Bi et al., 2017; Chan et al., 2020b) based on side-by-side comparisons of cell populations with similar expression levels (Figure 2A–C; see Materials and methods for details on expression measurements).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by comparative data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Multinucleated syncytia were detected in 18 of 24 decedents who died as a direct consequence of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Multinucleated syncytia were detected in 18 of 24 decedents who died as a direct consequence of SARS-CoV-2 infection (Figure 2D–H), a finding supported by other patient cohorts (Giacca et al., 2020; Tian et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by histological examination data shown in Figure 2D-H.

claim: Syncytia in COVID-19 patient lungs are of lung epithelial origin, as demonstrated by nuclear staining for TTF-1 (NKX2-1).
source: These syncytia were of lung epithelial origin, as demonstrated by nuclear staining for TTF-1 (NKX2-1) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Only one of nine decedents with diffuse alveolar damage from other causes demonstrated multinucleated syncytia.
source: In contrast, only one of the nine decedents with diffuse alveolar damage from other causes demonstrated multinucleated syncytia, indicating that these syncytia are not a common feature of lung inflammation (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by histological examination data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: Pathological syncytia are a direct consequence of pulmonary involvement by SARS-CoV-2.
source: Thus, pathological syncytia are a direct consequence of pulmonary involvement by SARS-CoV-2 (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the histological examination data comparing COVID-19 patients to controls.

claim: Syncytia in COVID-19 patient lungs were generally not positive for the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein.
source: These syncytia, however, were generally not positive for the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein, similar to previous reports (Bryce et al., 2020; Rockx et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunohistochemistry data and citations to previous reports.

claim: The U2OS-ACE2 heterokaryon assay has a Z'-factor of 0.85.
source: After careful assessment, the U2OS-ACE2 heterokaryon system was shown to be the superior assay based on its Z'-factor (0.85), a measure of separation between positive (spike RBD/ACE2 co-culture, no fusion) and negative (spike FL/ACE2 co-culture) controls (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D); generally Z'-factor > 0.5 is considered excellent for a high-throughput assay (Zhang et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by assay characterization data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Fusion was detectable by 1 hour in the heterokaryon assay, and Z'-factor peaked by 4-5 hours.
source: To determine an optimal time point for quantification, co-cultures were performed for 1–6 hr: fusion was detectable by 1 hr, and Z'-factor peaked by 4–5 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by time-course data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Nelfinavir was unique among tested protease inhibitors in blocking fusion.
source: Surprisingly, the antiretroviral protease inhibitor nelfinavir was unique in blocking fusion (Figure 3C), a compound whose therapeutic potential was identified by others (Musarrat et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No single endocytic route (clathrin, caveolae, macropinocytosis) was essential for fusion.
source: Notably, no single endocytic route (clathrin, caveolae, macropinocytosis) was essential (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F), and markers of each pathway did not co-localize with spike at sites of membrane-fusion or in the vesicles that resulted (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by drug screening data (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F) and co-localization studies (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Apilimod, a PIKFYVE kinase inhibitor, was particularly potent in preventing syncytia formation.
source: For example, apilimod, a promising COVID-19 drug candidate that inhibits PIKFYVE kinase (Cai et al., 2013; Kang et al., 2020; Riva et al., 2020), was particularly potent (Figure 3E), however less so than in the case of infection studies (Kang et al., 2020; Riva et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Inhibition of actin polymerization blocked fusion.
source: Inhibition of actin polymerization blocked fusion (Figure 3E), consistent with a putative role for cortical actomyosin-generated mechanical forces in fusion pore formation (Figure 1; Chan et al., 2020b; Shilagardi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by drug screening data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Several drugs that perturb membrane lipid composition were identified as fusion inhibitors (MBCD/lovastatin, genistein, nystatin).
source: Finally, several drugs that perturb membrane lipid composition were identified (MBCD/lovastatin, genistein, nystatin) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by drug screening data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Of ~6000 small molecules screened at 30 μM, 167 (2.8%) were inhibitory hits.
source: Of these, 167 (2.8%) were inhibitory 'hits', which signified non-toxic compounds with a decrease in fusion greater than 3-standard deviations from the mean (z-score<-3) (Figure 4B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by screening data shown in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The vast majority of the top-80 most potent compounds from the screen replicated in 7-point dose-responses.
source: To validate, we performed 7-point dose-responses for the top-80 most potent compounds, the vast majority of which replicated (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Hit compounds were more lipophilic (LogD) and featured a greater number of ring systems compared to non-hits.
source: Among several statistically significant differences, hits were more lipophilic (LogD) and featured a greater number of ring systems (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cheminformatics analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Little correlation was observed between EC50 values and lipophilicity of hit compounds.
source: Reassuringly, little correlation was observed between EC50 values and lipophilicity (Figure 4E), indicating that the trend is not a result of a general increase in lipophilicity with avidity, as is commonly observed for promiscuous compounds in phenotypic screens (Tarcsay and Keserű, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Two scaffold classes reached particularly high statistical enrichment in hit compounds: dicholorophenethyl-imidazoles (found in azole antifungals) and tetrahydropyran-containing macrocyclic lactones (found in both ivermectin- and rapamycin-like compounds).
source: Two scaffold classes (and corresponding substructures) reached particularly high statistical enrichment: dicholorophenethyl-imidazoles (found in azole antifungals) and tetrahydropyran-containing macrocyclic lactones (found in both ivermectin- and rapamycin-like compounds) (Figure 4C,F; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by scaffold enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4C, F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Replacement of spike's transmembrane and cytoplasmic domains with the B7 TM blocked fusion.
source: While 'chimeric' ACE2 similarly promoted cell fusion relative to wild-type (WT), chimeric spike protein lost this ability (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by co-culture data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Replacement of spike's transmembrane domain with single-pass TMs of unrelated proteins (B7, ITGA1) blocked fusion.
source: Replacement of spike's transmembrane domain with single-pass TMs of unrelated proteins (B7, ITGA1) blocked fusion, despite similar subcellular localization and ACE2-binding (Figure 5C,L; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by co-culture data shown in Figure 5C, L and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Removal of spike's COPII-binding, ER-Golgi retrieval motif (1–1268) had no effect on fusion.
source: Removal of its COPII-binding, ER-Golgi retrieval motif (Cattin-Ortolá et al., 2020; McBride et al., 2007) (1–1268) had no effect, nor did deletion of its subsequent acidic patch (1–1256) (Figure 5C,L; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by co-culture data shown in Figure 5C, L and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Removal of an additional 11 amino acids from spike's cytoplasmic domain (1–1245) decreased fusion, and further truncation (1–1239) completely blocked it.
source: However, removal of an additional 11 amino acids (1–1245) decreased fusion, and further truncation (1–1239) completely blocked it (Figure 5C,L; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by co-culture data shown in Figure 5C, L and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Relative fusion correlated with overall cysteine content of the spike cytoplasmic domain.
source: Relative fusion correlated with overall cysteine content of the CTD (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Of all proteins in viruses that infect humans, SARS-CoV-2 spike features the highest cysteine content in a 20-amino acid sliding window.
source: Of all proteins in viruses that infect humans, SARS-CoV-2 spike features the highest cysteine content, followed closely by spike proteins in related coronaviruses, then hepatitis E ORF3 (Figure 5G; Supplementary file 2); it should be noted that ORF3 is palmitoylated and critical to viral egress (Ding et al., 2017; Gouttenoire et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by bioinformatics analysis shown in Figure 5G and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Mutagenesis of all spike cysteines to alanine severely diminishes cell-cell fusion in both U2OS and Vero models.
source: Consistent with studies on similar coronavirus spike proteins (Liao et al., 2006; McBride and Machamer, 2010a; Petit et al., 2007), mutagenesis of all spike cysteines to alanine severely diminishes cell-cell fusion in both U2OS and Vero models (Figure 5I–L; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 5I-L and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Of thousands of human transmembrane proteins, only 15 were 'spike-like', featuring both high membrane-proximal cysteine and aromatic content.
source: Of the thousands of human transmembrane proteins, only 15 were 'spike-like', featuring both high membrane-proximal cysteine and aromatic content (Figure 5H; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by bioinformatics analysis shown in Figure 5H and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The top four 'spike-like' human proteins are all critical to forming specific types of adhesion junctions: three to tricellular tight junctions (ILDR1, ILDR2, LSR) and one to kidney/intestine tight junctions (IGSF5).
source: Remarkably, the top four are all critical to forming specific types of adhesion junctions: three to tricellular tight junctions (ILDR1, ILDR2, LSR) and one to kidney/intestine tight junctions (IGSF5) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D; Higashi et al., 2013; Hirabayashi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by bioinformatics analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and citations to relevant literature.

claim: RBD attached to the native TM/CTD of spike featured significantly reduced recovery in FRAP experiments compared to ACE2, B7 TM-anchored RBD, and B7 transmembrane control.
source: In contrast, RBD attached to the native TM/CTD of spike featured significantly reduced recovery, with FL spike displaying even slower dynamics (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 spike does not partition strongly into GPMVs' dense, ordered phase (Lo).
source: Given previous results using indirect detergent fractionation readouts (McBride and Machamer, 2010b; Petit et al., 2007), we were surprised to observe that SARS-CoV-2 spike does not partition strongly into GPMVs' dense, ordered phase (Lo) (Figure 6D), which is enriched for cholesterol and sphingolipids (Levental et al., 2009; Levental et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by GPMV partitioning data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Treatment with the raft-disrupting drug myriocin, which depletes sphingolipids from the plasma membrane, did not inhibit fusion.
source: Moreover, in our cell fusion assay, treatment with the raft-disrupting drug myriocin, which depletes sphingolipids from the plasma membrane (Castello-Serrano et al., 2020), did not inhibit fusion (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by drug treatment data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: Long-term culture caused spike (but not ACE2) to accumulate in immobile deposits on the glass surface of the culture dish.
source: Despite lack of partitioning into the cholesterol-rich ordered phase of GPMVs, we noted that long-term culture caused spike (but not ACE2) to accumulate in immobile deposits on the glass surface of the culture dish (Figure 6E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cholesterol markers co-localized with immobilized spike deposits.
source: We thus co-expressed the cholesterol-binding protein SCARB1 (Linton et al., 2017) with spike or stained spike cells with fluorescently labeled cholesterol. Both cholesterol markers co-localized with immobilized spike deposits (Figure 6E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Drugs that disrupt cholesterol synthesis (zaragozic acid) or reduce plasma membrane cholesterol (25-hydroxycholesterol; MBCD) inhibited fusion in a dose-dependent manner.
source: To interrogate the role of cholesterol in cell fusion, we tested drugs that disrupt cholesterol synthesis (zaragozic acid) or reduce plasma membrane cholesterol (25-hydroxycholesterol; methyl-beta-cyclodextrin or 'MBCD') in the U2OS-ACE2 heterokaryon assay. All compounds inhibited fusion in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: MBCD-conjugated cholesterol greatly enhanced fusion, unlike MBCD-conjugated linoleic acid and oleic acid.
source: Unlike MBCD-conjugated linoleic acid and oleic acid, cholesterol greatly enhanced fusion (Figure 6I; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 6I and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: A small subset of compounds, including allylamine antifungals (naftifine and terbinafine) and anesthetics (ropivacaine, bupivacaine, propofol), enhance fusion in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Indeed, a small subset of compounds, which include allylamine antifungals (naftifine and terbinafine) and anesthetics (ropivacaine, bupivacaine, propofol), enhance fusion in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6J; Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 6J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Apilimod inhibited pseudovirus entry at nanomolar concentrations but did not completely block it.
source: Apilimod, a PIKFYVE inhibitor and promising therapeutic in multiple SARS-CoV-2 models (Kang et al., 2020; Riva et al., 2020) including heterokaryon assays tested herein (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), inhibited (but did not completely block) entry at nanomolar concentrations (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by pseudovirus entry data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 25-hydroxycholesterol had no effect on pseudovirus entry.
source: By contrast, 25-hydroxycholesterol, which lowers plasma membrane cholesterol by redirection to the cell interior (Abrams et al., 2020; Im et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2020; Zang et al., 2020a; Zhu et al., 2020b; Zu et al., 2020), had no effect (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by pseudovirus entry data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: MBCD blocked pseudovirus entry.
source: However, MBCD, which directly 'strips' plasma membrane cholesterol without engaging intracellular targets (Zidovetzki and Levitan, 2007), blocked virus entry (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by pseudovirus entry data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Pre-treatment of cells with millimolar doses of MBCD had no effect on SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Pre-treatment of cells with millimolar doses of MBCD, which strongly inhibits both co-culture syncytia formation and pseudovirus entry, had no effect on infection as determined by RT-PCR and immunohistochemistry (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by SARS-CoV-2 infection data shown in Figure 7F-G.

claim: Pre-treatment of SARS-CoV-2 with low micromolar MBCD completely blocked infection.
source: In striking contrast, pre-treatment of SARS-CoV-2 with low micromolar MBCD completely blocked infection (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by SARS-CoV-2 infection data shown in Figure 7F-G.

claim: Cholesterol content of SARS-CoV-2 viral particles, but not the host cell, is critical to infectivity.
source: Therefore, cholesterol content of SARS-CoV-2 viral particles, but not the host cell, is critical to infectivity (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the differential effects of MBCD treatment on virus vs. cells (Figure 7F-G).

claim: The findings potentially provide a molecular basis for positive outcomes reported in COVID-19 patients taking statins.
source: Our findings potentially provide a molecular basis for positive outcomes reported in COVID-19 patients taking statins and suggest new strategies for therapeutics targeting the membrane of SARS-CoV-2 and other fusogenic viruses.
evidence: This is stated as a potential implication in the abstract, connecting the experimental findings to clinical observations.

claim: The findings suggest new strategies for therapeutics targeting the membrane of SARS-CoV-2 and other fusogenic viruses.
source: Our findings potentially provide a molecular basis for positive outcomes reported in COVID-19 patients taking statins and suggest new strategies for therapeutics targeting the membrane of SARS-CoV-2 and other fusogenic viruses.
evidence: This is stated as a potential implication in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: Retrospective analyses of patient outcomes observed significant reductions in mortality for those prescribed cholesterol-lowering statins.
source: Consistent with this, retrospective analyses of patient outcomes observed significant reductions in mortality for those prescribed cholesterol-lowering statins (Daniels et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to clinical studies (Daniels et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).

claim: A critical role for cholesterol in virus assembly may explain the observation that statins reduce COVID-19 mortality.
source: A critical role for cholesterol in virus assembly may explain this observation, and could partially account for why COVID-19 risk factors (e.g. menopause, obesity, age) (Costeira et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020) similarly correlate with differential sterol processing.
evidence: This is stated as an inference in the Discussion section, connecting the experimental findings to clinical observations.
